42864584.text: The increased utility of quantitative metrics in medical imaging has prompted the use of colour representation of the data. Colour schemes for image display can highlight pathology and distinguish normal anatomy, thus potentially aiding image interpretation. Adding colour schemes to images may serve the sole purpose of visualising an abnormality or may seek to represent and meaningfully convey a quantitative metric. An early use of colour representation is exemplified by colour Doppler in ultrasound (US), where a two-sided linear scale is commonly applied. More recently, many schemes have arisen, ranging from a single colour to depict a segmented region to a range of colours that embrace the entire colour spectrum. These may be applied as continuous or discrete palettes, depending on the software vendor or even on individual user settings. The lack of standardisation of colour schemes across the medical community, especially in medical imaging, risks misinterpretation of quantitative data and potential unintended negative clinical consequences. The purpose of this article is to review the colour schemes used for quantitative imaging across US, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), the way in which they are applied, the clinical applications where their use is desirable for enhanced interpretation, and the pitfalls where standardisation is lacking in a variety of clinical applications. Finally, we discuss some solutions that could be employed to enable standardisation and augment the use of colour in image interpretation. KEY POINTS: Question Colour schemes in medical imaging can highlight pathology, but standardisation is lacking for most imaging modalities, thus risking misinterpretation of quantitative data. Findings For T1, T2, and T2* maps and their inverses, colour map recommendations have recently been proposed, but are mostly lacking for other quantitative data. Critical relevance statement Standardised colour maps can enhance data analyses across scanners and institutions, which is important for multicentre studies and handling big data. Furthermore, standardised and harmonised colour maps could improve lesion conspicuity, cross-platform comparability, and longitudinal reliability.

43007084.text: Background MRI is central to multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis. Although 7-T MRI improves lesion detection compared with 3-T MRI, systematic head-to-head comparisons across lesion locations and key imaging biomarkers, including the central vein sign (CVS) and paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs), remain limited; consensus statements call for such studies to better define the clinical value of 7-T MRI. Purpose To systematically compare 7-T and 3-T MRI for detecting MS lesions across characteristic intracranial regions and key imaging biomarkers and to assess the incremental clinical value of 7-T MRI for lesion detection. Materials and Methods Patients with MS from the China National Registry of Neuro-Inflammatory Diseases were prospectively enrolled and underwent same-day 7-T and 3-T MRI examinations (March 2023 to June 2024). Images were anonymized and independently interpreted by two experienced raters in a blinded manner according to standard criteria. Lesion counts were compared with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; inter- and intrarater reliability were assessed with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Cohen κ, respectively. Results Among 30 participants (median age at MRI, 34.5 years [IQR, 30-48.3 years]; 27 female), 7-T MRI depicted more MS lesions overall than 3-T MRI (2268 vs 1779; relative increase, 27.5%; P < .001), with higher detection across cortical (+135.7%), juxtacortical (+26.1%), periventricular (+18.8%), and infratentorial (+33.5%) regions (all P < .001). Moreover, 7-T MRI visualized more CVS-positive lesions (1451 vs 592; +145.1%; P < .001) and more PRLs (634 vs 468; +35.5%; P < .001). The proportion of CVS-positive lesions was higher with 7-T MRI than with 3-T MRI (64.0% vs 33.3%, P < .001), whereas the proportions of PRLs were similar (28.0% vs 26.3%, P = .057). Interrater reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.99). Conclusion Compared with 3-T MRI, 7-T MRI improved MS lesion detection across characteristic intracranial regions and key imaging biomarkers, with a higher proportion of CVS-positive lesions but similar PRL proportions, supporting the clinical value of 7-T MRI.

43019234.text: 18F-FDG PET/CT findings of a giant ovarian endometrioma are exceedingly rare. We present a case of a 27-year-old woman with a giant pelvic cystic mass mimicking malignancy. 18F-FDG PET/CT revealed a massive cystic lesion occupying the entire abdominopelvic cavity, with mild internal septations and mild FDG uptake. Despite elevated tumor marker levels, weight loss, and suspicious imaging findings, the final histopathologic diagnosis was bilateral ovarian endometriomas.

43066784.text: Pancreatoblastoma is a malignant tumor, which accounts for less than 1% of all pancreatic neoplasms. Further, it is rarely seen in adults and has a poor prognosis with metastasis or local invasion is present in nearly half of adult patients at diagnosis, most often involving the liver. CT is the first-line modality for detection and surgical planning, yet the findings overlap those of more common pancreatic tumors. Pancreatoblastoma typically presents as a large exophytic mass in the pancreatic head with well-defined margins and an enhancing capsule. However, the capsule is often incomplete, and advanced tumors may show infiltrative borders. The mass is heterogeneous and may be solid or mixed solid and cystic, with calcification, enhancing internal septations, necrosis, hemorrhage, or potentially even internal vascularity. Pancreatoblastoma is mostly hypoattenuating relative to normal pancreatic parenchyma and shows progressive enhancement. Large tumors may cause biliary or main pancreatic ductal dilatation, tumor thrombus, or invasion of adjacent organs. Using pathologically proven adult cases, this pictorial review illustrates the spectrum of CT appearances of pancreatoblastoma and highlights the imaging characteristics of this rarely encountered tumor.
